query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting the heavy Hf with an equivalent amount of Zr in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its overall density while retaining its single‐phase BCC structure and the corresponding high strength at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g cm−3 and high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace Hf with Zr on a substitutional basis (either partially or fully) so that the alloy composition becomes, for example, MoTaTi with a higher fraction of Zr instead of Hf, maintaining equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under ambient conditions and under high-temperature loading (~1000 °C), using both tensile and compressive setups as appropriate to evaluate strength retention.
generation.structural_mediator: The similar atomic radii and chemical behavior of Hf and Zr are expected to preserve the single-phase BCC structure and solid solution strengthening mechanisms that provide high strength; however, the lower intrinsic density of Zr will lower the alloy’s overall density.
generation.mechanism: By substituting the heavier Hf (atomic weight ≈178.5) with the lighter Zr (atomic weight ≈91.2), the average atomic weight of the alloy is reduced. Since Hf and Zr are chemically and structurally similar, the solid-solution effects, lattice distortion, and consequent high mechanical performance should be maintained across the temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to have a significantly lower density compared to 10.21 g cm−3 while exhibiting comparable yield strengths and mechanical properties at room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a single-phase BCC structure and demonstrated high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to roughly 1000 °C; loading conditions applied consistent with standard tensile and compressive mechanical tests used for refractory HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal substitution level (full versus partial Hf replacement) that achieves the best balance between lowering density and maintaining mechanical properties is not predetermined. The phase stability and long-term high-temperature behavior of the modified alloy will need further confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a variant of the alloy where Hf is substituted with Zr using the same casting process as the original HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize the alloy’s phase structure via XRD and microstructural techniques. Measure its density and conduct mechanical tests (tensile tests at room temperature and compressive tests at ~1000 °C).
measurements: High temperature (~1000 °C) yield strength or compressive strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substituted alloy shows a reduction in yield strength or other mechanical properties (e.g., more than a 10% drop) compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if the single-phase BCC structure is not preserved, then the hypothesis is falsified despite any reduction in density.

Microstructure, Tensile and Creep Properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: This paper examines the microstructure and mechanical properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20. Two casting processes, namely, gravity casting and suction-assisted casting, were applied, both followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). The aim of the current study was to investigate the creep and tensile properties of the material, since the literature review revealed no data whatsoever regarding these properties. The main findings are that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings. The HIP process also led to a considerable increase in the mechanical properties of both materials under compression, with values found to be higher than those reported in the literature. Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C. Fractography yielded brittle fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation prior to fracture.

WxNbMoTa Refractory High-Entropy Alloys Fabricated by Laser Cladding Deposition

Abstract: WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys with four different tungsten concentrations (x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53) were fabricated by laser cladding deposition. The crystal structures of WxNbMoTa alloys are all a single-phase solid solution of the body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. The size of the grains and dendrites are 20 μm and 4 μm on average, due to the rapid solidification characteristics of the laser cladding deposition. These are much smaller sizes than refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated by vacuum arc melting. In terms of integrated mechanical properties, the increase of the tungsten concentration of WxNbMoTa has led to four results of the Vickers microhardness, i.e., Hv = 459.2 ± 9.7, 476.0 ± 12.9, 485.3 ± 8.7, and 497.6 ± 5.6. As a result, NbMoTa alloy shows a yield strength (σb) and compressive strain (εp) of 530 Mpa and 8.5% at 1000 °C, leading to better results than traditional refractory alloys such as T-111, C103, and Nb-1Zr, which are commonly used in the aerospace industry.
